evidence.text: it's important to build out a detailed spreadsheet breaking down everything: product, freight, packaging, duties, taxes, warehousing, platform fees, transaction costs, and payment transfer fees. If you want to understand your landed cost for customers, you'll also need courier fees. If you need help building the spreadsheet, just go to Chat TBT and prompt it asking for all of these hidden costs and then fill out the template. Alternatively, you can join Daily Mentor. We've got so many templates like this. So, when you know your real cost per unit, you can start making smarter choices everywhere else. Marketing spend, ad testing, even offer strategy, pricing, and negotiation. Once you understand your costs, it's time to focus on how pricing and negotiation really works. Most founders chase the lowest possible unit cost, thinking it's the key to profit, and end up sitting in warehouses full of unsold products. Sure, they saved $2 a unit, but they killed their cash flow in the process. Because you see, early on, flexibility is worth more than margin. Paying slightly more per unit gives you room to test, pivot, and adjust without overcommitting. Your first few production runs might not be about maximizing profit. They might be about learning, such as how fast does the stock sell, how consistent is quality, and where delays happen. Once you know those answers, that's when you can negotiate confidently. And remember, negotiation isn't just about price. It's about partnership. If you squeeze a supplier too hard, they'll make up the difference somewhere else, such as cheaper materials, skipped quality control, or sometimes even slower timelines. Factories have margins, too. And when they're under pressure, your brand usually pays for it later. Good negotiation means balancing what works for both sides. Now, no factory will ever lower their price or offer better payment terms unless they know that you have options. That's why it's smart to get quotes or samples from at least one other supplier. It keeps the conversation honest and gives you leverage without hostility. Be transparent about your goal. Share your forecast and show them your serious about scaling. Now that you know your margins and have your deal locked in, it's time to learn how to move that product. And that's where freight and fulfillment come in next. Chapter four, freight, customs, and fulfillment. Getting your product from the factory floor to your hands of your customers without losing your sanity or your profit can be very, very painful. Logistics is the bloodstream of your business. Every day your inventory sits idle, it's burning cash. Every time you touch it, it's burning cash. The faster and cleaner you can move your stock through the supply chain, the stronger your cash flow and the calmer your business will feel. Freight forwarders and planning lead times. There are really only two ways to move your product. Air or C. Air is fast and expensive, which is perfect for small or urgent batches or if you've got a tiny product. C is slower but dramatically cheaper. It's what keeps your margins healthy once you're scaling. Most successful brands use a hybrid strategy. Air freight, a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow up with C shipments to restock at lower cost. But this really depends on your product size and weight. For small items, a mix works well. For larger or heavier items, C freight is almost always the best option. But moving stock isn't just about picking a transport method. It's about planning lead times backwards. Freight isn't instant. Sea can take 30 to 40 days doortodoor. Air might take 7 to 10 and production itself can often add another 20 or 30 days. That means that if you wait until you are nearly out of stock to reorder, you're already too late. Start planning your next shipment the moment your current one lands. The biggest reason brands panic ship or run out of stock isn't bad luck, it's just bad forecasting. From the moment your PO is signed, your countdown begins. You need visibility from factory to warehouse at all times. That's where freight forwarders come in. These companies manage the complex stuff for you. Booking containers, handling customs, and coordinating delivery to your warehouse. A good forwarder will update you before problems happen and help you navigate global delays. If you've ever tried to handle shipping yourself, you know it's chaos. Different time zones, customs forms, endless email chains. A strong forwarder simplifies all of that. They'll quote you based on route, wait, and deadlights. And more importantly, they'll tell you what's realistic. And again, don't always chase the cheapest rate. The cheapest freight forer might leave your goods sitting at a port for weeks and fill a container instead. Finally, before that container leaves the factory, book your final inspection. This is your last chance to catch mistakes before they multiply. A $200 QC check, quality control check, can save $20,000 in damage or inconsistent stock in that last check stage. Your QC agent will test random units, check measurements, verify packaging, labeling, and carton weight. And they'll take photos of everything. [music] They'll flag even small inconsistencies that could become massive issues later. If they find problems, the factory can fix them before the shipment leaves. Once it's on the water, it's just too late. You need to think beyond just product quality and more about protecting your reputation and customer experience. Think of it like insurance, a small cost that keeps your entire operation safe. You approve or reject the shipment based on that report and only release final payment once everything passes. Fulfillment and 3PLs. If all goes smoothly and your goods arrive, your job still isn't finished. It's now just shifted from production to delivery. Disorganization can kill brands at this step. You need to learn more about 3PL's. A 3PL, also known as third party logistics provider, is the bridge between your factory and your customers. They store, pick, pack, and ship your orders, manage returns, and often integrate directly with Shopify or your warehouse management tools. However, the difference between a good 3PL and a bad one can make or break your experience with e-commerce. When we were scaling the Udy, fulfillment became our biggest threat overnight. During one of our Q4, we were forecasting record numbers, $45, $50 million in sales, and everything looked perfect until one of our 3PL collapsed under the pressure. We lost tens of millions in potential revenue and even ended up in the news because customers thought we were scamming them. It was one of the hardest lessons that I've ever learned. That experience made me realize how critical fulfillment partners are. You can do everything right, product, marketing, sourcing, and still lose it all if your logistics partner fails you. So, how do you pick the right one? Don't just compare prices or promises. Ask questions that really expose how they operate, such as accuracy. What's their error rate on orders shipped? Speed. How fast do they process during peak volume and how do they do that? Communication. Who's your direct contact when problems [music] actually hit? Scalability. How have they handled previous Q4 surges for other brands? And never skip going to visit their warehouse to see how it all operates. Once you've seen two or three, you realize who the true players actually are. You also want to ask them how do they handle returns, damages, and restocks. Do they flag issues proactively or wait for you to notice? Those answers tell you who will protect your brand when orders start flying. Our coaches at Daily Mentor always hammer home that fulfillment isn't a set and forget system. It's a living part of your business. The best operators track inventory turnover weekly, maintain shared dashboards with their warehouses, and hold monthly reviews with their 3PL partners. These habits prevent the exact disaster we went through. Once you built a setup like this, your logistics should start to feel very, very calm. And that's the goal, predictable, repeatable, and reliable. When fulfillment runs on autopilot and nothing feels urgent, that's when you know it's working. Next, let's look at the final piece of the puzzle. Forecasting, cash flow, and reordering. How do you actually keep up this whole system running without ever running out of stock again? [music] Chapter 5, forecasting and planning. You might think the hardest part of sourcing is over once your product is shipping smoothly and orders are being fulfilled. But that's actually where most brands slip. Everything you've built up to this point, your supplier relationships, your logistics, your product quality, only matters if you can keep it consistent. A lot of founders treat forecasting like an afterthought, but it's one of the most important parts of sourcing. Because sourcing isn't just about finding great products. [music] It's about keeping them in stock, profitable, and moving through your supply chain. If you followed everything up to now, this is the final step that ties it all together. This part will decide whether your sourcing process scales or collapses. The real cost of poor planning. Back in the early days of the Udie, I thought we had it all figured out. Our products were selling fast, ads were converting, and everything looked like it was working perfectly. But then co hit. I remember watching sales skyrocket overnight, $200,000 days back to back and thinking we'd hit the jackpot. But I didn't realize how big the demand spike would be. Within a week, we were completely sold out. It doesn't sound like a problem, right? Wrong. We had zero stock, monthsl long production lead times, and no forecasting system in place to keep catching up. cards.title: Choose freight mode and plan lead times backward
cards.claim: Air is fast and expensive and is described as perfect for small or urgent batches or tiny products; C is slower but dramatically cheaper and helps keep margins healthy once scaling. The passage states most successful brands use a hybrid strategy: air freight a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow up with C shipments to restock at lower cost. For small items, a mix works well; for larger or heavier items, C freight is almost always the best option. Sea can take 30 to 40 days door-to-door, air might take 7 to 10, and production can add another 20 or 30 days, so planning must go backward from lead times.
cards.action: Select air, C, or a hybrid based on product size, weight, and urgency; plan lead times backward and start planning the next shipment the moment the current one lands.

When deciding between air and C freight
When planning reorders and lead times
do_not_use_when: For larger or heavier items, do not treat air as the default; the passage says C freight is almost always the best option.
Do not wait until nearly out of stock to reorder.

cards.title: Book pre-shipment QC and release final payment after pass
cards.claim: Before the container leaves the factory, book a final inspection. A $200 QC check can save $20,000 in damage or inconsistent stock in that last check stage. The QC agent tests random units, checks measurements, verifies packaging, labeling, and carton weight, takes photos, and flags inconsistencies so the factory can fix problems before shipment. Approve or reject based on the report and release final payment only once everything passes.
cards.action: Book the final inspection before the container leaves the factory; use the QC report to approve or reject the shipment and release final payment only if it passes.
applies_when: Before a shipment leaves the factory
When you need a last chance to catch mistakes before they multiply
do_not_use_when: Once the shipment is on the water, it is too late for this pre-shipment inspection.
unknowns: QC provider selection, sampling method details, and acceptance criteria are not specified.
The $200 cost and $20,000 savings are presented as an example, not a guarantee.
evidence_quotes: Finally, before that container leaves the factory, book your final inspection.
A $200 QC check, quality control check, can save $20,000 in damage or inconsistent stock in that last check stage.
Your QC agent will test random units, check measurements, verify packaging, labeling, and carton weight.
If they find problems, the factory can fix them before the shipment leaves. Once it's on the water, it's just too late.
You approve or reject the shipment based on that report and only release final payment once everything passes.
